summary.text: Simple harmonic motion is a periodic motion in which the restoring force is directly proportional to the object's distance from equilibrium.
A mass on a spring following Hooke's law is the classic example, and it moves back and forth in a smooth sine pattern.
It also models small pendulum swings and molecular vibration, and it underpins the study of more complicated periodic motion.

facts.label: Hooke's law
facts.value: Spring force is proportional to the displacement

facts.label: Isochronous
facts.value: Period does not depend on amplitude

facts.label: Circular link
facts.value: It is a projection of uniform circular motion

facts.label: Period formula
facts.value: T = 2 π √(m/k) for a mass on a spring

items.prompt: You stretch a spring twice as far as before. What happens to the pull that tries to bring it back?
items.explain: In simple harmonic motion the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement from equilibrium.

items.prompt: A mass on a spring passes straight through the resting point instead of stopping there. Why?

options.label: The restoring force is strongest at that point
It has gained momentum from the restoring force
The wall pulls on the spring

items.explain: At equilibrium the net force vanishes, but the mass has momentum from the earlier acceleration, so it continues past and compresses the spring.

items.prompt: You compare a big stretch and a small stretch of the same spring and mass. How do the times for a full back-and-forth compare?

options.label: The big stretch takes about the same time
The big stretch takes much longer
The big stretch takes much less time
The small stretch never completes a cycle

items.explain: Simple harmonic motion is isochronous: period and frequency do not depend on amplitude.

items.prompt: Someone hangs an extra constant weight on a spring-and-mass system. What does that do to the period of the bouncing?
items.explain: An additional constant force cannot change the period of oscillation.

items.prompt: A bulb on a spinning wheel is lit from the side, so you only see its shadow moving along a wall. How does the shadow move?

options.label: In a sudden jerk each turn
In a path that never repeats

items.explain: Simple harmonic motion is the one-dimensional projection of uniform circular motion.

items.prompt: A mass on a spring loses energy to friction. How does its motion differ from true simple harmonic motion?

options.label: The oscillation fades, which is damped oscillation

items.explain: With no energy loss the mass keeps oscillating, but if energy is lost it exhibits damped oscillation.
